selection_rationale: Full original longitudinal investigation of Argentine fiscal, monetary, external and social inflation mechanisms from national monetary formation and the 1890 banking collapse, through 1975, 1989–90, 1991–2001, 2018 and the observed 2024–September 2026 period, distinguished from existing concise country overview and 1991 policy case.
contrary_evidence: Nineteenth-century banking and exchange crises do not establish uninterrupted high CPI inflation since independence; chronic inflation primarily consolidated after 1945.
The 1991 peg genuinely achieved rapid disinflation before later collapse under external and debt constraints.
The 2018 sudden stop and 2001 crisis demonstrate debt and currency vulnerabilities not captured by money growth alone.
The inflation slowdown observed in 2024–2025 does not by itself resolve the reserves, growth, debt and income-distribution constraints.
2007–15 CPI/GDP reliability and methodological breaks limit long-run series comparability.
limitations: Historic monetary regimes and selected postwar inflation observations cannot be joined to modern nationally representative CPI as a homogeneous series.
Observed year-end 2023–2025 annual inflation, September 2026 monthly CPI and May 2026 IMF forecasts have distinct time frequencies and evidentiary status.
INDEC poverty refers to 31 urban agglomerations and half-year comparisons require seasonal and methodological care.
Fiscal, monetary, currency, wage indexation and external effects are not attributed an unsupported constant quantitative weight across different historical regimes.
Bibliography includes repeated foundational publications to align explanatory source use; distinct source counts must use unique works and hosts.
